question: Why do MAD hyperparameters transfer from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 but not to Mixtral?
asked_by: Smit et al., Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
remaining_question: Why do MAD hyperparameter settings (such as agreement intensity) tuned on GPT-3.5 transfer to GPT-4 but not to Mixtral 8x7B: the sparse-MoE architecture, or model-specific differences in conformity and instruction following? Testable by re-tuning the hyperparameters per model and comparing transfer on matched MoE/dense pairs, measuring whether realized agent behaviour follows the prompted setting.

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: Re-tune MAD hyperparameters such as agreement intensity per model, compare transfer on matched MoE and dense model pairs, and measure whether the agents' realized behaviour follows the prompted setting.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.08296v3: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
findings.claim: In controlled evaluations of single- vs multi-agent architectures, the authors report that the optimal coordination pattern differs across OpenAI, Google and Anthropic model families and call coordination efficacy contingent on each family's 'intrinsic communication bandwidth and reasoning alignment'; they say the precise mechanisms 'remain to be characterized' and list candidate factors (instruction-following fidelity, context utilization, inter-turn consistency). The same paper also reports architecture-specific scaling slopes differing by at most 0.023 across families, which it reads as model-agnostic scaling.
findings.setting: Experiment; three LLM families: OpenAI (GPT-5-nano, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5), Google (Gemini-2.0 Flash, Gemini-2.5 Flash, Gemini-2.5 Pro) and Anthropic (Claude Sonnet 3.7, Claude Sonnet 4, Claude Sonnet 4.5; Sonnet 3.7 not on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench); 260 configurations over benchmarks including Finance, SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench; multi-agent system (MAS) configurations such as Centralized and Hybrid compared with SAS systems at matched maximum total iterations. Differs from the question: not multi-agent debate on QA, no agreement-intensity hyperparameter, and no Mixtral among the listed models.
findings.bears_on: Whether multi-agent configurations carry over across model families, and candidate (untested) mechanisms other than architecture.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2606.00820v1: Not All Flips Are Conformity: Decomposing Stance Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
findings.claim: Decomposing answer changes in debate into spontaneous instability, stance-induced conformity and reasoning-induced persuasion, the authors report substantial model-dependent instability across three model families, and that the relative contribution of spontaneous degradation versus harmful conformity to accuracy loss varies across models (GPT-4o, Qwen, DeepSeek), depending on 'model-specific stability characteristics'.
findings.setting: Experiment; multi-agent debate with counterfactual controls (self-reflection, stance-only, reasoning exposure); primary setting GPT-4o on MMLU-Pro, robustness on GPQA-Diamond and two further families (DeepSeek, Qwen). No agreement-intensity prompt, no Mixtral.
findings.bears_on: Gives a measurable model-specific property (instability vs conformity) through which a prompt-level agreement setting could act differently across models; the paper does not test hyperparameter transfer.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2609.35875v1: Beyond Symmetric Agents: Cognitive Diversity and Multi-Agent Debate in Small Language Models
findings.claim: A debate study over 23 open-weight models spanning dense, mixture-of-experts and hybrid architectures notes that its pool contains an MoE-versus-dense pair (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B vs. 27B) but leaves integrating it into the team design to future work.
findings.setting: Experiment; 23 open-weight models (0.6B-109B total parameters) from eleven vendor families and three architecture types (dense transformer, mixture-of-experts, hybrid state-space/attention); multi-agent debates, with model-diversity teams drawn from 19 of the models under a fixed, stratified team design; a three-model judge panel (Gemma3-27B-it, GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B) that never participates in debates scores the biography task. Differs from the question: the quoted lines concern team composition, not whether a tuned MAD hyperparameter (such as agreement intensity) transfers across GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Mixtral.
findings.bears_on: Smit et al.'s architectural (MoE) hypothesis: still untested in this later study.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2502.08788v3: Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate -- We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
findings.claim: Re-evaluating MAD frameworks against CoT with four models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b, Claude-3.5-haiku), the authors report that MAD methods fail to consistently outperform CoT across different models and benchmarks, and that EoT's advantage over CoT on GSM8K and CommonsenseQA was observed only when using Claude-3.5-haiku among the four models. When varying the number of agents or debate rounds, the sole notable exception was EoT on GSM8K, where increasing the number of agents from 3 to 9 led to a continuous improvement, ultimately surpassing CoT; aside from this exception, increasing the number of agents or debate rounds often resulted in stagnation or even a decline, so superior performance over CoT across various benchmarks could not be realized by merely adjusting hyperparameters. They rule out suboptimal hyperparameter configurations as 'a universal explanation' for MAD's inferior performance compared with CoT.
findings.setting: Experiment: re-evaluation of MAD frameworks (including EoT and SoM) against CoT with four models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b, Claude-3.5-haiku) on benchmarks including GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, MMLU and HumanEval; in the hyperparameter analysis the number of agents (e.g. 3 to 9) and debate rounds (e.g. 2 to 4) are varied, and the quoted lines do not say which model was used there. Differs from the question: the hyperparameters varied are agents and rounds, not agreement intensity, and there is no GPT-3.5-to-GPT-4 or Mixtral transfer test.
findings.bears_on: Model-dependence of MAD gains (one method's advantage did not carry across models) and the role of agents/rounds hyperparameters; no explanation of non-transfer.
